Cache Design Walkthrough: Product Details

Applying everything to a 50K read-QPS product page: requirements, estimation, per-field policy, and read/write/outage flows.

RequirementsEstimationPer-field TTLSingle-flightOutbox invalidation

Quick Revision

  • Different fields, different freshness: metadata 10 min, price 30-60 s, browse stock 2-5 s, checkout = source.
  • 50K QPS, 80% cacheable, 95% hits → origin still sees 12K QPS; size the DB for that plus failure headroom.
  • 10M keys × 2.2 KB × RF 2 ÷ 70% ≈ 63 GB → provision ~80 GB.
  • Read: L1 → L2 → single-flight → DB → CAS fill with version + jittered TTL.
  • Write: DB + outbox in one transaction → versioned invalidation → return version token.

Requirements → decisions

AskAnswerDecision
Peak reads / writes?50K / 500 QPS (100:1)Shared L2, optional L1; cache-aside
Latency?Page p99 < 50 ms; cache < 5 msIn-region L2, compact values
One TTL for all fields?NoSeparate metadata, price, stock, recs keys
Seller read-after-write?YesSession bypass or min-version token
Traffic skew?Flash sale 1,000×L1, hot-key replication, single-flight, CDN
Cache loss?Degrade OK, DB overload notBounded fallback, stale, shedding
Multi-region?Local reads, home-region writesRegional caches, versioned async invalidation
Personalized fields?SomeScope in key or don't share
Invalid IDs common?YesShort negative cache + Bloom filter

Estimation

cacheable = 50,000 × 0.80        = 40,000 QPS
hits      = 40,000 × 0.95        = 38,000 QPS
misses    = 40,000 × 0.05        =  2,000 QPS
origin    = 10,000 + 2,000       = 12,000 QPS  (76% offload)

latency (cacheable) = 0.95×2 + 0.05×(2+40+3) ≈ 4.15 ms
latency (overall)   = 0.80×4.15 + 0.20×40    ≈ 11.3 ms  (average, not p99)

memory  = 10M × 2.2 KB ≈ 22 GB → ×2 RF ≈ 44 GB → ÷0.70 ≈ 63 GB → ~80 GB
egress  = 38,000 × 2 KB ≈ 76 MB/s
expiry  = 10M ÷ 3,600 s ≈ 2,778/s (1 h TTL) → jitter + bounded refresh

getProduct(key, minVersion):
  v = L1.get(key); if usable(v, minVersion): return v
  v = L2.get(key); if usable(v, minVersion): L1.put(v); return v
  return singleFlight(key, () =>
    v = L2.get(key)                       // double-check
    if usable(v, minVersion): return v
    row = db.read(key)
    L2.compareAndSetIfNewer(key, envelope(row, row.version), jitteredTTL)
    L1.put(key, ..., shortTTL)
    return row)
  • Write - validate + idempotency key → one transaction: row + outbox with new version → commit → return version → publisher sends at least once → consumers invalidate L2 and broadcast L1 → dedupe by event ID/version → retry, DLQ, alert. TTL is the final safety net.
  • APIs - GET /v1/products/{id}?region&storeId&locale, PATCH /v1/products/{id}; cache API: get, multiGet, set(value, ttl, version), delete, CAS.

Interview practice

Answer aloud, then reveal.

Microsoft Senior SE (Mar 2026): LRU with TTL, made concurrent.

HashMap + doubly linked list for O(1) LRU; min-heap/timing wheel or lazy expiry for TTL; sharded/striped locks with atomic list moves.

Walmart (Dec 2024): LLD a modular, scalable cache.

Cache<K,V>, Storage, EvictionPolicy, Clock, optional Loader; inject LRU/LFU/FIFO. HashMap + DLL for O(1) LRU; sync, TTL, size limits, tests.

Amazon: cache latest value per key with timestamped history; nearest-timestamp lookup.

Per key, an ordered map by timestamp; O(log n) out-of-order insert; floor/ceiling lookup and choose nearest; define ties, retention, memory bounds, locking.

How do you guarantee fresh inventory at checkout?

Don't use the browse cache; validate/reserve against the authoritative inventory with idempotency and concurrency control.

Should the cache be a REST service?

Usually a native client or thin library; a proxy can centralize routing, but a REST wrapper adds hops and serialization. Namespaces prevent collisions.
